Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)
Progress towards poliomyelitis eradication, WHO Western
Pacific Region, January 1996-September 1997
In 1988, the World Health Assembly adopted the goal of
global poliomyelitis eradication by the year 2000. This goal
was subsequently endorsed in each of the 6 WHO Regions,
including the Western Pacific Region (WPR). Since 1988,
substantial progress has been achieved towards this goal.
In WPR, the reported incidence of poliomyelitis decreased
from 5 963 cases in 1990 to 197 cases in 1996. This report
documents the progress of the poliomyelitis eradication

summary.text: Begins a bilingual English–French Weekly Epidemiological Record report on progress towards polio eradication in the WHO Western Pacific Region, January 1996 to September 1997, noting cases fell from 5,963 in 1990 to 197 in 1996. It describes routine oral polio vaccine coverage rising to 95% and the start of supplementary immunization activities.

summary.text: Describes national and sub-national immunization days across the polio-endemic countries of the Western Pacific Region and high-risk response immunizations to eliminate the last reservoirs, focused on the Mekong delta and Tonle Sap area of Cambodia and Viet Nam. It also begins reporting acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance results for 1997. The report text is given in parallel English and French.

blocks.content: Bilingual (English/French) map of Cambodia, southern Lao People's Democratic Republic and southern Viet Nam showing districts included in high-risk-area immunization activities (HRRIs), May–July 1997 (shaded), and locations of wild poliovirus in 1997 (stars), most around Phnom Penh and in Cambodia. Labels give children immunized: 75 000 in Lao PDR, 1.1 million in Cambodia and 1 million in Viet Nam.

summary.text: Reports that 9 of 3,796 acute flaccid paralysis cases in 1997 were confirmed as wild poliovirus, mostly in Cambodia with one in Viet Nam, and that no wild virus had been found since March 1997. It is followed in French and includes a map caption for high-risk immunization areas.

blocks.title: Page 5
blocks.content:
All recently endemic countries (except for Papua New
Guinea) have reached or exceeded the WHO-established
minimum rate of AFP indicating a sensitive surveillance
system (at least 1 non-poliomyelitis AFP case per 100 000
children aged under 15 years [Table 1]). Except for Papua
New Guinea, the percentage of AFP cases from which
2 specimens were collected within 14 days of onset of
paralysis (“adequate specimens”) is projected to reach at
least 60% by the end of 1997 for all recently endemic
countries. This important indicator is exceeding 80% in
Cambodia, China and Viet Nam.
Laboratory network

summary.text: Reports that most recently endemic countries met the minimum AFP surveillance rate and stool-specimen targets, Papua New Guinea being the exception. It describes the regional polio laboratory network, its proficiency testing and faster turnaround of virus typing results. It then turns to certification of polio eradication, with the English text repeated in French.

blocks.content:
Enhanced surveillance has been critical to target in-
tense immunization activities to the last areas with known
or suspected circulation of wild poliovirus. Detailed and
timely information on AFP cases is now available to pro-
gramme managers, and rapid action has been taken
wherever wild virus transmission is suspected. The map-
ping of key surveillance data (i.e. distribution of “polio-
compatible” AFP cases) and detailed immunization cover-
age information were essential in identifying high-risk
areas for HRRIs in Cambodia, the Lao People’s Demo-
cratic Republic and Viet Nam in 1997. Detai

summary.text: Discusses lessons from the Western Pacific polio programme, including the use of surveillance mapping to target high-risk immunization areas, detailed district-level planning, and active AFP case searching in health facilities. It explains how these measures improved sensitivity and timeliness. The French version follows, ending with steps countries are taking to prevent any new indigenous wild-virus case from 1998.

summary.text: Concludes the bilingual polio report, noting regional confidence in near-certification standards but concern about sustaining surveillance, funding and national priority until global certification. It credits the source as a WHO Western Pacific Regional Office report also published in MMWR.
